title: Kander
place: Kander cut at Strättligen, into Lake Thun
summary: Bern led the Kander through a hill into Lake Thun to stop floods in the villages below Thun.
why: The Kander comes down from the Bernese Oberland with much gravel. Before 1714 it ran across the flat land west of Thun and joined the Aare below the town. There its gravel narrowed the Aare and held back its water. Villages such as Thierachern, Uetendorf and Uttigen were flooded again and again. Water backed up to Thun and Lake Thun, and the flat shore land became marshy.

In early 1711 the government of Bern decided to lead the river into Lake Thun, where the gravel could settle in deep water. Samuel Bodmer made the plan and led the work, which lasted from 1711 to 1714.

The work solved one problem and made new ones. The tunnel fell in, and the river cut a deep gorge. Nobody had studied what the extra water would do to Lake Thun. The lake now got much more water, and Thun suffered floods. Bern had to widen the Aare outflow in Thun, and work on the Aare down to Bern went on for about 150 years. The Kander diversion was the first large river correction in Switzerland.
gained: Lake Thun now catches the flood peaks and the gravel of the Kander. The Aare below Thun down to Bern got clear relief from floods.
Large areas west and north of Thun could be drained. The flooded gravel plain between Gwatt and Uttigen became farmland, and later settlements were built there.
lost: The river cut a deep gorge through the hill by backward erosion (the river bed wears away upstream). This erosion still threatens bank protection on the lower Kander today.
The flood danger moved to the shores of Lake Thun. Thun had large floods and needed very expensive new works from 1720 to 1726.

Later corrections on the same river (from 1899) destroyed most of its floodplain habitat. Over 40 weirs and sills block fish, and the lake trout of Lake Thun became threatened. In 2009 a plan for the river was finished, and the canton now plans river widenings.

stops.title: The Kander before 1714
text: Before 1714 the Kander did not flow into Lake Thun. The red dashed line shows its old course: north through the valley of today's Glütschbach, then across the Thun Allmend (common pasture). It joined the Aare below Thun, opposite the mouth of the Zulg.

The red area shows the wide gravel bed on the Allmend. The river carried much gravel and had little slope here. It often flooded Thierachern, Uetendorf, Uttigen and other villages, and its gravel pushed water back up the Aare to Thun.
The lower part of the line is approximate. Switch on the historical map of 1890 to see the old river bed. The old bed is still marked there as 'Kandergrund'.

stops.title: A tunnel through the hill
text: Bern decided to lead the Kander into Lake Thun. The map maker Samuel Bodmer made the plan.

From 1711 to 1713 about 300 day workers and 100 forced labourers dug a tunnel of about 250 m through the Strättlig hill. In August 1714 the hill above the tunnel fell in. The river then quickly cut a deep gorge backwards into the land.
The blue line shows the new short course through the gorge into the lake. The red dashed line shows the long old course to the Aare, which became dry.

Old course of the Kander before 1714: Glütsch valley and across the Thun Allmend to the Aare (lower part approximate)

stops.title: Now Thun is flooded
text: All the Kander water now came into Lake Thun. Its inflow rose by more than 60 percent. The lake rose, and the town of Thun had big floods.

From 1720 to 1726 Thun made the Aare canal (the 'new Aare') wider and opened it. It also rebuilt bridges and the town water works. Work on the locks in Thun and on the Aare down to Bern went on for about 150 years.
The blue line shows where the Kander water now enters the lake. The red dashed line shows the old course, which no longer brought water to the Aare below Thun.

Old course of the Kander before 1714: Glütsch valley and across the Thun Allmend to the Aare (lower part approximate)

stops.title: Gravel from the delta
text: The Kander built a delta (new land made of river gravel) into Lake Thun. The blue line shows the river across this delta.

Since 1913 the company Kanderkies AG takes gravel from the delta, so the delta has kept about the same size. In 1930 a church meeting centre was built on the delta, today the Gwatt-Zentrum. In 1974 a nature area, the Unterer Kandergrien, was made at the lake.

title: Lungerersee (lowered and dammed again)
summary: Lungern lowered its lake by 18 m through a tunnel to win farmland (1790–1836); in 1921 a power station dammed the lake again and the new land went back under water.
why: Lungern had little flat land. To win farmland, the commune lowered its lake. From 1790 to 1836 people dug a tunnel of about 420 m through the rock ridge at Kaiserstuhl. The lake fell from about 675 m to 657 m above sea level, and about 170 ha of new land appeared, mostly at the south end near the village. One older study gives other figures (35 m lower and 90 ha of land); here the HLS figures are used.
The new land brought problems. The streams that flow into the lake now had a lower end, so they cut deeper into their beds and damaged the new fields.

In 1921 the lake was dammed again for the Lungerersee power station (run by the CKW power company, concession 1919). Since then the level moves between 667.5 m and 692 m. The level never falls back to 657 m, so the lowest part of the land won in 1836 stays under water. At high water the lake is higher than before 1790.
gained: The lowered lake gave about 170 ha of new farmland at Lungern (1836).
Since 1921 the dammed lake feeds the Lungerersee power station, which makes electricity.
lost: The streams into the lake now cut deeper. Their erosion damaged the new fields.
In 1921 the lake was dammed again, and the lowering was partly undone. Part of the won land went back under water.
The power station makes the lake level go up and down. At low water a bare strip of shore without plants appears.

title: Linth
place: Lake Walen to Lake Zurich (with the Escher canal from Mollis)
summary: The Linth was led into Lake Walen and a new canal was dug to Lake Zurich, to end floods, marshes and malaria in the Linth plain.
why: In the 18th century the bed of the Linth in the plain rose by several metres. Forest cutting in Glarus was long blamed for this, but a later study doubts it. From the 1750s the gravel blocked the Maag, the outflow of Lake Walen, at Ziegelbrücke. Lake Walen rose, and Weesen and Walenstadt stood in water for weeks or months. The plain became a marsh with malaria, and people lost their best land.

Andreas Lanz of Bern made the first plan to lead the Linth into Lake Walen (HLS gives 1783; he presented it to the Tagsatzung in 1784). In 1804 the Tagsatzung (the meeting of the cantons) decided to do the work. It was paid by shares that cantons, communes, firms and many private people bought. Hans Conrad Escher of Zurich led the work from 1807 and took no salary. He died in 1823, and in the same year he and his male descendants got the name 'von der Linth'.

The Linth correction is called a national work. After about 200 years the Linth works were out of date. The project 'Linth 2000' (planned from 1998, approved in 2007, last appeal rejected in 2008) renews them and gives the river more room in some places.
gained: The Linth plain and the Walensee area were protected from floods. The level of Lake Walen fell a lot, and the dykes held in the floods of 1999 and 2005.
The land flooded and marshy between 1750 and 1850 could be farmed again. Later drainage (1942–1962) made the plain a farming region.
Marsh fevers (malaria and similar fevers) disappeared from the plain.
lost: The marshes and moors of the plain disappeared. The later drainage of the plain added to this loss.
Below Ziegelbrücke the canal runs above the land between dams. Side streams cannot flow into it, so they need parallel ditches and a pumping station.
The straight canals left little room for nature. The project Linth 2000 (approved in 2007, last appeal rejected in 2008) gives some back with large river widenings and new habitats.

stops.title: A plain of marsh and fever
text: Before 1807 the Linth flowed from Mollis to Ziegelbrücke. There it met the Maag, the outflow of Lake Walen. Then it wound through the Linth plain to Lake Zurich. The red dashed line shows this old course.

From the 1750s gravel from the Linth blocked the Maag. Lake Walen rose, and Weesen and Walenstadt were flooded again and again. The plain became a marsh (red area near Tuggen). Malaria (a fever spread by mosquitoes) hit the villages.

The long red line comes from a plan of 1811 and is approximate. The short red lines near Tuggen are old river arms that were still on the map in 1890. Switch on the historical map of 1854 to see the old river bed.

stops.title: The Escher canal
text: Andreas Lanz from Bern had the idea in 1783: lead the Linth into Lake Walen. The lake would catch the gravel.
The work began in 1807. Johann Gottfried Tulla from Baden helped with the plan. Hans Conrad Escher led the work with Conrad Schindler.
In 1811 the Escher canal opened (blue line). It is about 5 km long and leads the Linth from Mollis straight into Lake Walen. The red dashed line shows the old bed to Ziegelbrücke.

stops.title: The Linth canal
text: In 1816 the Linth canal opened (blue line). It leads the water from Lake Walen straight through the plain to Lake Zurich, at Grynau.
The red dashed line shows the winding old river. Lake Walen now catches the gravel and the floods. The level of Lake Walen went down, and the towns on the lake were safe from the yearly floods.

text: The marsh in the plain was drained step by step (red area: the old marsh near Tuggen). The upper plain became farmland during the Second World War. The lower plain followed until 1965.

title: Aare between Thun and Bern
summary: In two corrections (1824–1859 and 1871–1892) the canton of Bern narrowed the Aare between Thun and Bern from about 400 m to about 50 m, to win land and to make the river usable for boats all year.
why: Between Thun and Bern the Aare once flowed in a bed up to about 400 m wide, with many channels and islands of gravel. Large parts of the valley floor could not be used, because the river and its floodplains spread over them.

In the 18th and 19th centuries the population grew fast. People needed more farmland and room for villages. The Aare was also an important transport route, and boats and rafts were to use it all year. For these reasons the canton of Bern corrected the river twice: from 1824 to 1859 and from 1871 to 1892. The bed was narrowed to about 50 m between dykes.

For about 100 years the corrected river worked well, and houses, roads and wells were built close to it. But the narrow, fast river dug its bed deeper, and since the Kander has flowed into Lake Thun (1714) almost no new gravel comes down. The groundwater sank. After the large floods of 1987 people began to think differently about rivers; there was another large flood in 1999. The canton then started the project 'Hochwasserschutz Aare Thun–Bern', which widens the river in places and gives it natural banks again.
gained: The valley floor between Thun and Bern became safe farmland. For about 100 years people could build close to the river without much danger.
Settlements, roads, railways and drinking-water wells were built in the former river area.
lost: The wide bed with channels, islands and floodplain forests was lost. People later saw the loss of bank trees, floodplain forest and species as a serious loss.
The narrow, fast river dug its bed deeper (bed erosion). The groundwater fell strongly, and drinking water was lost.
Much value was built next to the river, so floods like 1999 caused more damage. Since the 2000s widenings and side arms give the Aare some room back.

A slide in the 2026 presentation suggests the 1871-1892 work was mainly the stretch just below Thun and 1824-1859 the stretch down to Bern; this split is read from a sketch and not certain. title: Hinterrhein in the Domleschg
summary: The canton of Graubünden put the Hinterrhein in the Domleschg into one straight bed, filled the old gravel bed with silt to make farmland, and tamed the Nolla torrent above Thusis.
why: The Hinterrhein in the Domleschg had a wide gravel bed with many arms. The Nolla torrent at Thusis made it worse: it dumped mud and stones into the Rhine, dammed it up to 12 m high, and then the water broke out over the valley. Escher of the Linth already wrote about the Nolla after the flood of 1807.

Richard La Nicca, the first cantonal engineer of Graubünden, made the plan in 1826. Work began in 1832. Dams held the river in one bed from Cazis to Rothenbrunnen, and silt from the Nolla filled the old bed to make farmland. The floods of 1868 to 1870 set the Rhine works back three times. So from 1870 the canton, with money from the Confederation, built big stone check dams in the Nolla gorge, planned by Adolf von Salis and built under Friedrich von Salis. The big dams and many smaller ones were finished by 1902.
The Rhine work was finished in 1892. The Nolla never stopped moving: its catchment is unstable, and the canton still repairs the old dams today.
gained: The river works gave the valley protection from floods. After the Nolla check dams (from 1870), the Nolla no longer dammed up the Hinterrhein.
The old gravel bed was split into fields and filled with silty Nolla water (colmation: letting muddy water settle). Much good farmland was won.
lost: The wide river with many arms became one straight, built-up channel. The stretch Thusis–Rothenbrunnen is strongly marked by the works; only below Rothenbrunnen a natural relic remains.
The Nolla catchment never came to rest. The canton must still repair damaged check dams today.

title: Seyon (Neuchâtel)
place: Through the town of Neuchâtel, from Vauseyon to the lake
summary: In 1843 the town of Neuchâtel diverted the Seyon so that its mouth lies 600 m further west. New streets could then be built on the old river bed in the centre.
why: The Seyon comes down from the Val-de-Ruz through a gorge and once ran right through the town of Neuchâtel to the lake. The town grew along its banks. A great flood on 8 October 1579 carried away the town hall and almost all the town archives.

The work was paid with the fortune that the merchant David de Pury left to the town. In 1843 the river was diverted (led away). It now runs through a tunnel, and its mouth moved about 600 m to the west.
The old bed in the centre was filled in. New quarters grew on it, and a street there still carries the river's name: the Rue du Seyon.
gained: The diversion freed the old river bed in the centre. New town quarters were built on it.
A street now runs where the river flowed: the Rue du Seyon.
lost: The Seyon no longer flows through the town. Its bed in the centre was filled and built over.

title: Reuss in Uri
summary: Uri put the Reuss into a straight canal to the lake, which won farmland; in 1985 a natural delta was made again.
why: The Reuss is the main river of the canton of Uri. It often flooded the flat valley floor between Altdorf and Lake Uri. Because of this, land owners formed groups to build and keep river banks. A special court for water works on the Reuss and the Schächen is known from 1493. The state of Uri paid part of the costs.

From 1850 to 1863 the Reuss was put into a canal from the Attinghausen bridge down to the plain. From 1900 to 1912 the canal was made longer at the mouth. The straight river gave more land for farming. In the first half of the 20th century the plain on both sides was drained. In 1891 the river became property of the canton.

The Reuss carries about 100,000 m3 of gravel each year. Since 1891 companies have taken this gravel out of the lake. The dredging ate away the shore. Land of the Korporation Uri at the delta became smaller and smaller.

In 1985 the canton of Uri made a law on the Reuss delta. The canal was made shorter and two side arms were opened. Now the Reuss flows into the lake in three branches and can build a natural delta again. The gravel company had to dig so that no more land was lost, and new islands were made in the lake. In August 1987 a big flood broke the dams and covered the Uri Reuss plain. From 1995 to 1999 the canton built new flood protection between Flüelen and Attinghausen.
gained: The canal made more land usable for farming. In the early 20th century the plain on both banks was drained.
Since 1985 the shortened canal and two opened side arms let the Reuss build a natural delta again. New shallow water areas formed and the shore stopped eroding.
lost: Below the Seedorf bridge the first canal was too narrow. Floods broke the dams in 1860 and 1868. After the canal was widened in 1869, the bed began to rise.
Gravel taken from the lake since 1891 made the shore erode, and land at the delta was lost. The 1985 delta project stopped this loss.
In 1987 a flood broke the dams and covered large parts of the valley floor. New flood protection followed from 1995 to 1999.

title: Broye (Moudon to Lake Morat)
summary: In 1853–1856, soon after the flood of 1852, the Broye was straightened between Payerne and Lake Morat; from 1892 to 1906 the stretch from Moudon to Payerne followed, and the wet valley became farmland.
why: The Broye is a slow river with many bends. Since the Middle Ages, forest clearing had covered its plain with a thick layer of mud. The river flooded the valley often; big floods came in 1852, 1876, 1888, 1895 and 1944.

In 1853–1856, the year after the flood of 1852, the river between Payerne and Lake Morat was straightened and embanked. The cantons of Vaud and Fribourg worked together on it. A second stage between Bressonnaz near Moudon and Pont Neuf near Payerne followed in 1892–1896 and 1898–1906, after the floods of 1876, 1888 and 1895 (Vischer gives 1891–1908 for this stage). Smaller works came later at Villeneuve (1916–1918) and Fétigny (1924–1933).
The corrections changed the whole valley. Large fertile areas were put under the plough.
gained: The valley was completely changed: large fertile areas were put under the plough. The Broye plain became farmland.
lost: Soon after the first canal, the bed near Pont Neuf cut about 3 m deeper, partly by backward erosion (the bed wears away upstream). Floods still came 11 to 20 times per decade until 1878.

The straight, embanked river lost contact with its floodplain. In Fribourg, works like these strongly reduced natural diversity. In 2019 Fribourg presented a project to give a 3 km stretch at Surpierre a natural course again.

title: Gürbe
summary: The canton of Bern put the meandering Gürbe into a straight canal and drained the marshy Gürbe valley.
why: The Gürbe comes from the Gantrisch area and flows north to the Aare. In the 18th century people cut forests in the mountains for alpine pastures. After that the upper river became wild, and the flat valley below flooded even more often. There the river made many bends. The marshy valley floor was used as pasture and for growing cabbage.

In 1854 the canton of Bern took over the river works. A straight canal with side ditches was built in the valley, and forests and check dams were made in the mountains. The costs were shared between the federal state, the canton and the landowners.

The canal and later land improvements made the valley dry, so fields, a railway and later an airfield could be built. Floods still came, for example in 1990. After the floods of 1995 the mouth of the Gürbe was rebuilt and its floodplain made more natural, but along most of the river there is little room for this.
gained: The canal and side ditches drained the marshy valley floor. The Gürbe valley became a region of fields and vegetables.
The dry valley made room for a road, the Gürbetal railway (1901–02) and the Belpmoos airfield (1929).
lost: The marshy valley floor, used as pasture, was drained and lost.
Floods and landslides still came, for example in 1990. The Gürbe became one of the most expensive torrents in Switzerland, and renaturation is only partly possible.

title: Seez
summary: The Seez was corrected so that the Seez valley, made marshy by floods and a high Lake Walen, could dry out.
why: The Seez comes from the Weisstannental, leaves the valley at Mels and flows about 12 km to Lake Walen at Walenstadt. Floods of the Seez hit Mels in 1750, 1762, 1764 and 1817. At the same time the level of Lake Walen rose more and more. So the floor of the Seez valley turned into marsh.

The Linth correction (1807–1816, led by Hans Conrad Escher) lowered Lake Walen. By 1865, after more work at the outflow, its flood level was about 4 m lower. This was the first help for the Seez valley.

The second step was the Seez correction from 1855 to 1865. A corporation (Seezkorporation, today the Seezunternehmen) carried out the work to drain the valley. Walenstadt joined it in 1858. Industry came to Walenstadt only after the Seez canal was built, from 1862. The HLS (2010) says the Seezunternehmen still maintains the river works; a cantonal report of 2026 says the canton maintains the river and the Seezunternehmen manages the drainage network.
gained: The Linth correction lowered Lake Walen, and the Seez correction (1855–1865) followed. Together they stopped the valley from becoming a marsh and drained the Seez valley.
Industry came to Walenstadt only after the Seez canal was built, starting with a weaving mill in 1862.
lost: The corrected Seez still flooded, with larger events in 1910, 1922, 1953 and 1987. The 1987 flood led to a new flood protection project.
Floodplain forest is now a rare habitat in the Seez valley. The current flood project plans to give some land back to the river's own dynamics.

title: Nozon / Orbe
place: Orny and Orbe to Lake Neuchâtel
summary: Vaud put the Orbe and the Nozon between dams to drain the marshy Orbe plain and fight marsh fever.
why: The Orbe plain is very flat and lies only a little above Lake Neuchâtel. For centuries it was a marsh with peat soil, and marsh fever (malaria) was common.

In 1854 the Grand Council of Vaud decided to put the Orbe between dams. In 1856 the canton built new canals. Then the first Jura water correction (1869–1891, according to the HLS) lowered the lakes, which also helped to drain the plain.
The plain became farmland. But drained peat shrinks and sinks, so some farmland was lost for good. Today some valuable marsh habitats remain.
gained: The canals of 1856 pushed back marsh fever (malaria) in the Orbe plain.
Farmland appeared on the former marsh. In 1899 the Bochuz prison with its large farm was built on it.
lost: Drainage, pumping and the sinking of the peat soil caused a permanent loss of farmland by the end of the 20th century.
The large marsh disappeared. Only some valuable marsh habitats remain for insects, birds, wild boar and deer.

title: Alpine Rhine (Landquart–Rüthi)
summary: St. Gallen, with federal money, put the wide, braided Rhine between straight dams from Bad Ragaz to Au (1862-1883), to stop floods and to win dry farmland.
why: The Rhine brings much gravel from the mountains of Graubünden. In the flat valley the water slowed down and dropped the gravel. So the river bed and the ground water rose, and the fields beside the river became wet. The river had big floods, for example in 1566 and 1762, and many floods between 1817 and 1890.

For centuries each village protected itself with a 'Wuhr' (a short dam that pushes the water away from the bank). But a Wuhr on one bank pushed the water to the other bank. So the villages on the two banks of the Rhine quarrelled about their Wuhre for hundreds of years. In 1847 St. Gallen and Liechtenstein agreed on fixed bank lines and a river width of 120 m.

After many flood years from 1846 to 1856, St. Gallen passed a Rhine law in 1853. From 1862 the Swiss federal state paid one third of the cost. The engineers Friedrich Wilhelm Hartmann and Jost Wey built continuous dams from Bad Ragaz to Au (1862-1883). Inland canals and drainage followed.

The work gave dry farmland and safer villages. But it also destroyed almost all floodplains and moors. Later, gravel mining lowered the bed too much. The dam break near Schaan in 1927 showed that the dams were not safe everywhere.
gained: The continuous dams protected the St. Gallen side. After the works the only larger dam break was in Liechtenstein in 1927.
Wet land beside the river became farmland. The first large land improvement in Switzerland was made at Haag from 1885 to 1887, linked to the new inland canals.
Before the works there were no bridges from Tardis to Lake Constance. During the works 10 wooden bridges and one steel bridge were built.
lost: The natural river arms and floodplains disappeared, and the valley moors were drained. Moors covered 6039 ha in 1890 but only 106 ha in 1999.
Wetlands, groundwater-fed streams and floodplain forest shrank. Gravel mining from 1953 to 1972 lowered the bed by 4–5 m, and groundwater recharge fell.
In 1927 the dam broke near Schaan, and the Rhine flooded northern Liechtenstein.

stops.title: The natural Alpine Rhine
text: Before about 1860 no continuous dams held the Rhine in the St. Gallen Rhine valley. The river ran in a wide gravel bed, in places more than 500 m wide. It split into many channels around gravel banks and islands, and big floods moved its channel.

Below Au the river made long bends: around Diepoldsau and Hohenems, past Lustenau and Brugg, then west to Gaissau and Rheineck. It reached Lake Constance at Altenrhein, several kilometres west of today's mouth.
The red line and the red area are traced on the oldest swisstopo maps, the Dufour sheets of 1850 to 1854. The red line is the main channel; the red area is the whole gravel bed.

stops.title: Dams at Buchs and Sevelen
text: St. Gallen passed a law for a full Rhine correction in 1853. In 1862 the federal parliament agreed to pay one third of the cost. From 1862 the engineers Friedrich Wilhelm Hartmann and later Jost Wey built the works from Bad Ragaz to Au.

They built two straight dams. The water now ran in one channel between them. At Buchs and Sevelen you see the new dams (blue) and the old, wide bed (red) next to each other. Switch on the historical map of 1876 to see both on the map of that time.

stops.title: A straight river
text: By 1883 the dams reached from Bad Ragaz to Au. The old side arms dried out. Former flood land behind the dams became farmland.

But the dams closed the river off, so the side streams could not flow into the Rhine any more. So the Werdenberg inland canal (a river bed dug by people) was built in 1882-1886. It collects the small streams and leads them along the valley. In 1885-1887 the first large land improvement in Switzerland drained the land at Haag near Sennwald.

text: Today the valley floor is farmland, villages, roads and industry. The natural river and most wetlands are gone. In 1890 there were 6039 ha of moorland, in 1999 only 106 ha.

The dams did not end all danger. In 1927 the Rhine broke its dam above the railway bridge at Schaan and flooded the Liechtenstein lowland. Between 1953 and 1972 so much gravel was taken from the river that its bed sank by 4 to 5 m.

title: Rhône (Rotten)
summary: After the floods of 1860 the Rhône was put between dams from Brig to Lake Geneva. Two more corrections followed because the bed kept rising.
why: The Rhône carries much gravel from its many side streams. In the flat main valley of Valais it moved from one side of the valley to the other and made side arms and marshes. The plain was a danger for health (marsh fever) and for traffic, and little of it could be farmed. Each village built its own small dams, with little coordination. Some dams pushed the water to the other bank; after 1833 the canton's Rhône commission banned them.

The great flood of 1860 started the first correction. In 1860 Valais asked the young federal state for help. In 1863 the Confederation agreed to pay one third of the cost. It was the first time that Valais got federal money for a building project. The federal law of 1877 on river works later gave the Confederation a larger role in river works.

Because the bed kept rising with gravel, a second correction followed (about 1930–1960; the canton dates it from 1936). After the floods of 1987, 1993 and 2000, Valais and Vaud began the third correction (the canton gives 2009 or 2010 as the start). It makes the river bed wider or deeper and makes the river more natural in places. It needs farmland: in the public consultation of 2008 there were demands to use less farmland.
gained: The dams gave the Rhône plain some safety from floods. Bridges built after the correction resisted the floods.
The correction won about 7000 ha of fertile land for vines, fruit and vegetables. Farming grew, new jobs came, and fewer people left the valley.
Drainage of the marshes won much land. Before, diseases like malaria (marsh fever) spread on the wet valley floor.
lost: The dams did not stop the gravel. The bed rose higher and higher, so a second correction (1930–1960) made the river even narrower.
The narrow channel left little room for plants and animals. Since 2009 the third correction widens the river and brings back some natural banks.

stops.title: The first correction
text: After the floods of 1860, the Rhône from Brig to Lake Geneva was corrected from 1863. Two dams of earth or gravel were built 70 to 120 m apart (the HLS); an older study gives 72 to 96 m (Vischer). Short cross walls (groynes) pointed into the river and made a narrow main channel.

The blue line shows the river between its dams. The red dashed line and the red area show the old wide bed. For the first time the canton of Valais got federal money for a building project. Over time about 7000 ha of farmland were won for vines, fruit and vegetables.

text: The river could not carry all the gravel from its side streams to the lake. The bed rose again. Floods came in 1897 and 1935.

In the second correction (about 1930–1960) workers removed gravel from the bed and made the dams stronger and higher. Between Sierre and Martigny they joined the ends of the groynes to a firm bank (1928–1961). The blue line shows this fixed channel.

text: Floods in 1987, 1993 and 2000 showed that the dams were not safe enough. In 2000 a dam broke at Chamoson.

The third Rhône correction started in Visp (the canton gives 2009 on one page and 2010 on another). The blue line shows the Rhône at Visp. The river gets more space, and its bed is made wider or deeper.

notes: Dates differ: HLS table 1863–84, HLS Rhone article 1863–1894, canton 1863–1894; second correction HLS 1930–1960, canton 1936–1961. 'Until about 2040' is from a news summary of the canton plan (2020–2039 second stage), not checked on the canton page. The 1870 map already shows the first dams near Fully (work started 1863). Lines: old main channel Martigny–Riddes traced on the 1862 Dufour map (the 1870 sheet already shows first dams near Fully); delta arms placed by hand on the 1850 Dufour map; areas drawn by hand (approximate). New lines from OpenStreetMap ('Le Rhône', 'Rotten'). Farmers' protests against land loss for the third correction: general knowledge, not checked in a source. Gained/lost: No source names lost species or a lost area of floodplain forest for the Rhône; lost 2 relies on HLS saying the river 'should again' offer habitat (implying a loss) plus the general HLS statement on drained floodplains. The Valais state archive says systematic drainage of the plain often came only after World War I, so the land gain was slow. BAFU says malaria raged in the marshy valley floor but does not say the correction ended it; the item avoids that claim. Sources check: Flood of 1846 added (Vischer; HLS lists 1469, 1640, 1740, 1778, 1860). Dam spacing: HLS 70–120 m, Vischer 72–96 m; both given. 'At the cost of the next village' replaced by the ban on Schupfwuhren (Vischer). 'Federal laws of 1874–1877' changed to the law of 1877 (Vischer). 'Until about 2040' was wrong: BAFU says less urgent works start about 2040; HLS says planned for 30 years. Farmers' protests replaced by the consultation demand of 2008 (canton key dates). Third correction start: canton gives 2009 and 2010; BAFU 2010. Chemical industry in Visp removed (HLS names Lonza in Visp, but not as the reason for the works). First correction: HLS table and BAFU 1863–1884; HLS Rhone article, Vischer and canton 1863–1894. Bed lowering: the canton rejected a general lowering in 2009 (groundwater), but its works page says 'widen or deepen'; text says 'wider or deeper'.

title: Aare in the Hasli valley
summary: The Aare below Meiringen was put into a straight canal, and the marshy valley floor was drained.
why: The Hasli valley floor between Meiringen and Lake Brienz is flat. The Aare often changed its course from one side of the valley to the other, flooded the valley and kept it marshy. Farmers could not use the land well.

On 1 February 1866 the parliament of the canton of Bern decided to correct the river and drain the valley. Work started in autumn 1866 and gave the Aare a straight bed between dams. The HLS table gives 1866–1875; the canton says the work reached the Aare gorge in 1879 and ended in 1889.

The straight canal made the land dry. Today villages, fields, roads, the railway and the military airfield of Meiringen lie on the valley floor. The old dams have aged, and the canton plans to renew the whole work, also for nature.
gained: The correction protected the valley floor from floods. For over 100 years the canal did its job very well.
The correction made it possible to drain about 113 ha of the marshy valley floor. The land became usable for farming.
lost: The river lost its natural space. Roads and the railway now run on or at the foot of the dams, so there is no room to widen it.
The straight bed has few structures and is poorly linked to its side streams. Fish find few good habitats, also the lake trout (Seeforelle), whose main spawning area is here.
The old dams aged and became weak. The floods of 1987, 2005 and 2011 showed the deficits, so the canton plans to renew the whole work.

title: Alpine Rhine from Chur to the Tardis bridge
place: Chur (Plessur mouth) to the Tardis bridge near Landquart
summary: After the flood of 1868, the Rhine from Chur to the Tardis bridge was put between dams (finished 1892), so that the wide gravel bed near Untervaz and Trimmis became a narrow river.
why: Above Landquart the Alpine Rhine carries much gravel from its source rivers and torrents, and the gravel raised its bed. Between Chur and the Tardis bridge it spread over a wide gravel bed. The railway of 1858 and the villages of Trimmis and Untervaz lay close to it.
The great flood of 1868 hit many parts of Switzerland, also the Rhine valley. After it Richard La Nicca carried out the correction from Chur to the Tardis bridge, which was finished in 1892.

The correction won farmland, for example at Haldenstein. The river lost its wide gravel bed and floodplain forests. Since 1995 an international commission of the cantons, Liechtenstein, Vorarlberg and the two states coordinates all work on the Alpine Rhine.
gained: After the flood of 1868 the Rhine was corrected near Haldenstein, and new farmland was won.
lost: In the Alpine Rhine valley the corrections brought big ecological losses. Natural waters and floodplains (Auen) disappeared, and the valley moors were drained.
In the Chur Rhine valley the river was fixed between bank works for over 100 years. It dug its bed 3 to 5 m deeper and put dams and bridge foundations at risk.
The narrow channel had few gravel banks. A widening at Chur/Felsberg (1994–1996), just upstream, gave some back, and the rare common sandpiper (Flussuferläufer) has bred there since 2004.

notes: HLS says the correction between Chur and the Tardis bridge was realised by La Nicca after the flood of 1868 and finished in 1892; it gives no start year, so "1868" in built is the flood year. La Nicca was then over 70 and no longer cantonal engineer (he left that post in 1853), so his exact role is unclear. The gravel bed is traced on the Dufour-type map of 1859. Gained/lost: Thin on the gained side. No source I opened states that the Chur–Tardis dams protected the railway, road or villages; that safety gain is therefore not listed. The HLS Haldenstein article (Haldenstein lies on this stretch) is the only land-gain source. HLS Rhein's loss statement covers the Alpine Rhine valley floors in general, and its numbers on moors (6039 ha in 1890, 106 ha in 1999) seem to refer mainly to the St. Gallen Rhine valley, so they are not used. The Felsberg widening is just upstream of Chur, in the same 'Churer Rheintal', not inside the Chur–Tardis stretch; its bed-erosion figure covers the Churer Rheintal. HLS describes gravel raising the bed in the 19th century; the later incision is probably linked to gravel mining too (not checked for this reach). Sources check: Summary: 'Graubünden built' changed to passive (HLS names La Nicca only). why 3: 'dams protected railway, road' removed (no source); farmland gain at Haldenstein kept. Railway 1858 now from Vischer BWG 2003. Felsberg widening dates 1994–1996 from the GR sheet photo captions.

title: Zihl (Nidau–Büren canal)
place: Lake Biel to Büren an der Aare
summary: As part of the first Jura water correction, a wide canal replaced the winding Zihl below Lake Biel, so the lake could drain fast.
why: Lake Biel drained only through the slow, winding Zihl. At Meienried the Zihl met the Aare. When the Aare was high, it pushed its water back into the Zihl, so Lake Biel could not drain. The three Jura lakes rose, and the Seeland was flooded again and again.

The doctor Johann Rudolf Schneider pushed for a big solution for decades. The engineer Richard La Nicca made the plan. In 1867 the federal parliament agreed to pay 5 of the 15 million francs, and the cantons Bern, Fribourg, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Solothurn paid the rest. The Nidau–Büren canal was one of the main works of 1868–1891.

The canal helped to lower the lakes strongly; in 1887 a weir at Nidau was added. But the drained peat soil sank, and floods came back. So the canal was enlarged in the second correction of 1962–1973. Since 1939 the weir at Port regulates the lakes.
gained: The canal let Lake Biel drain faster. Together with the other works of the Jura water corrections, it brought relief from the floods.
The canals brought economic gains: new land and better shipping.
lost: At Meienried the Aare and the Zihl had made a dynamic floodplain. After the canal was built and the water fell, the area became still water, and several side channels filled up.
After the canal opened, Lake Biel sometimes fell lower than wanted. Banks started to slide and shores collapsed, so a weir was built at Nidau in 1887.

title: Aare and the Jura water corrections
place: Aarberg to Lake Biel (Hagneck canal), with the Broye and Zihl canals between the lakes
summary: The Aare was led into Lake Biel and the three Jura lakes were lowered and linked, to stop floods in the Seeland and win the Grosses Moos for farming.
why: The Seeland between the three Jura lakes is very flat. The Aare from Aarberg brought much gravel and flowed slowly to Meienried. There it blocked the Zihl, the outflow of Lake Biel. At high water the lakes rose and flooded the Grosses Moos and the land down to Solothurn. People suffered from floods, wet fields, poor harvests and marsh fever.

Johann Rudolf Schneider, a doctor and politician born in Meienried, fought for a solution. Plans existed from the 1830s. In 1841 and 1842 Richard La Nicca proposed to lead the Aare into Lake Biel through a canal at Hagneck, so the lake could catch the floods, and to lower all three lakes. In 1867 the federal state gave 5 of the 15 million francs. The cantons Bern, Fribourg, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Solothurn paid the rest. The work ran from 1868 to 1891.

The lakes went down by about 2.5 m, and new land came out of the water. St. Peter's Island became a peninsula. But the drained peat shrank, so the land sank and floods came back. The second correction (1962–1973) widened the canals. Today the soil loss in the Grosses Moos and the losses for nature are big problems.
gained: The regular floods in the plains around and between the lakes stopped.
The Grosses Moos, once a marsh, became farmland after drainage canals and pumps were built. Today it is known as the vegetable garden of Switzerland.
Before, poverty and marsh diseases (malaria) troubled the Seeland. In the Orbe plain the new canals pushed back the marsh fever.
The lower lakes freed a wide sand bank on Lake Neuchâtel. It became the Grande Cariçaie, the largest lakeshore wetland in Switzerland.
lost: The Grosses Moos was the largest moor area of Switzerland, about 100 km2, and an important home for plants and animals. Drainage turned it into fields, and the old river landscape disappeared.
The drained peat (soil made of old plant remains) breaks down in the air. It loses 1 to 2 cm per year, and in places the ground has already sunk 2 m.
The sinking land and poor lake control brought floods back, for example in 1910, 1944 and the 1950s. A second correction (1962–1973) was needed.

stops.title: The Hagneck canal
text: Richard La Nicca made the plan, and Johann Rudolf Schneider pushed for it. Work began in 1868. For the first time steam diggers were used on a large scale. Cranes and rail wagons moved the earth.

The Hagneck canal (opened 1878) leads the Aare from Aarberg west into Lake Biel (blue line). The lakes now hold back the flood water. The Nidau–Büren canal drains Lake Biel. The Broye and Zihl canals link the lakes of Morat, Neuchâtel and Biel. The red dashed line shows the old Aare, which became a quiet side water.
The lake levels went down by about 2.5 m. The blue areas along the shores show land that came out of the water. The floods stopped, and the Grosses Moos became farmland.

Opening year 1878 and the lake lowering of about 2.5 m come from secondary sources (HLS Hagneck article not read; sources say 2.5 m to almost 3 m). 'Vegetable region' is general knowledge. The 1975 map was not viewed for the Grosses Moos itself. Old Aare line and bed area traced automatically on the blue water of the 1880 Siegfried map, checked by eye. Land-gain areas: water on the 1880 (Lake Biel, Lake Morat) and 1892 (Lake Neuchâtel) Siegfried maps minus water on today's map; small slivers removed; outlines are good to about 30 m but some shore detail is lost. Grosses Moos outline drawn by hand (approximate). Canal lines from OpenStreetMap. La Nicca plan year 1842 and the 1867 federal decree: general knowledge consistent with HLS, not checked line by line. Gained/lost: The Orbe quote (HLS 008759) is about the Orbe plain canals, which belong to the same lake system; HLS does not tie it directly to the Jura correction, hence scope 'region'. No source says malaria in the Seeland ended because of the correction; the Vischer/BWG book says malaria disappeared from Switzerland around 1900 in general. The 2 m sinking is from Pro Natura Bern (an NGO) and is local ('stellenweise'). The SO fact sheet also says the lowering revealed prehistoric pile-dwelling sites (a possible extra gain, not used). Sources check: why 2: Schneider was born in Meienried (SO fact sheet), not 'from Nidau'; federal share stated as 5 of 15 million (SO fact sheet); La Nicca plans 1841/1842. why 3: 'loss of wetlands' widened to 'losses for nature'. Stop 2: 'work railways' replaced by cranes and rail wagons; 'lake catches gravel' removed (not in sources). Stop 3: 'lowered Lake Neuchâtel again' was wrong; the 2nd correction lowered the highest levels by 1 m and raised the lowest (SO fact sheet). Lake lowering 2.5 m and Hagneck canal 1878 now from SO Faktenblatt 3 (2023).

title: Landquart in the Prättigau
place: Schiers to Grüsch (and down to the Rhine)
summary: Dams and silt filling from 1870, and a straight canal built in 1912-1918, took the wide gravel bed of the Landquart between Schiers and Grüsch and turned it into farmland.
why: The Landquart comes down from the Silvretta and brings much gravel. In the open part of the Prättigau, between Schiers and Grüsch, it spread over the valley floor in many arms. Floods in 1464, 1762, 1910 and 1927 did heavy damage.

From 1870 dams and colmation works (fields filled with river silt) were built. The canal of 1912-1918 then fixed the river in one narrow bed. It gave farmland and protection, and it helped the economy of the valley.

Later engineers saw the downside: in the narrow bed the water ran faster and dug the bed deeper, and the river lost its natural banks. So in 2008-2011 the communes of Schiers and Grüsch widened the river again at four places.
gained: Dams and colmation (fields filled with river silt) from 1870 won about 2 million m2 of farmland by 1900.
The canal of 1912–1918 served land gain and flood protection. It helped the economy of the region a lot.
lost: In the narrow, straight bed the water ran faster and dug deeper. The bed sank, and bank works were undercut in places.
Valuable habitats for fish and other water animals and floodplain areas were lost. Since 2008–2011 four widenings double the bed width in places and give the river back some room.

title: Emme
summary: After centuries of local dams, the Emme was corrected step by step and its side streams were secured, to stop gravel-rich floods in the Emmental.
why: The Emme drains the hills of the Emmental. After storms it brings floods full of gravel. For centuries it broke out from time to time and destroyed land and houses. Poor people lived on the risky flat land along the river.
For a long time each village built its own dams, and often pushed the water to the neighbours. Bern made common rules in 1766–1768. After 1800 many forests were cut, and the floods got worse.

The federal laws on forests (1876) and water works (1877) brought federal money from 1884. Solothurn had started on its stretch in 1871, Bern started in 1886. Forests were planted and the river was put between dams. The river then cut its bed deeper, so today the banks need constant repair, and the cantons give the Emme more room in some places.
gained: The correction protected the factories and settlements along the lower Emme better from floods. This sped up industrial growth.
In the straight bed the water ran deeper and faster, so the river carried more gravel. At first it lowered its own bed, which was wanted.
lost: The river kept cutting deeper, because it got too little gravel from above. This undercut bank works and bridge piers, and today banks need constant repair.
Real floodplain forests along the Emme largely disappeared. Timber forests with no link to the river took their place.
The canalised Emme was only 25 to 30 m wide and had few gravel banks. In 2010–2020 Solothurn widened it up to 70 m in places, with flat banks and gravel islands.

title: Thur
summary: Thurgau and Zurich communes cut the bends of the Thur and built dams (1874–1893), after many floods in the Thur valley.
why: The Thur often left its bed, mostly in its middle course. Big floods came in 1664, 1755, 1789, 1852, 1876, 1881 and 1883. The yearly floods kept people from settling on the valley banks.

From 1874 to 1893, the communes along the river in Thurgau and Zurich worked together on one project, the Thur correction. Workers cut through the bends and built dams, so the river ran in a straight channel. The floods of 1876 and 1881 came while this work was going on. Who paid how much is not confirmed by a source we could open. Near the mouth, Zurich says a 5 km canal from Kleinandelfingen to the Rhine was built in about 1860.
The straight river did not stop all floods. Dams broke again in 1910, 1965, 1977 and 1978. The canton of Zurich also says that the protection works upstream sent more water down to the lower Thur.

In 1979 the three cantons on the river made a common plan. From 1983 to 2005, Zurich rebuilt the Thur from the Thurgau border to Andelfingen in a more natural way, in five stages. From 2008 to 2017, the project at the Thur mouth gave the river space again (the HLS gives 2007 as the start). Now it can make bends and flood its floodplain (the low land next to a river that water covers in a flood). The Thurauen are the largest floodplain area of the Swiss Mittelland, with almost 400 ha.
gained: The yearly floods had kept people from settling on the valley banks. The correction made the flood danger more predictable.
lost: In the straight bed the water ran faster and deeper, so the bed sank. This put the groundwater of the region and the few remaining floodplain forests at risk.
The uniform channel offered hardly any breeding or spawning places for water birds, fish and small water animals.
Floods still came, for example in 1910 and 1978. From 2008 to 2017 the Thur mouth project let the river meander and flood its floodplain again.

title: Limmat (Zurich to Dietikon)
place: Zurich-Altstetten to Oetwil an der Limmat
summary: After the floods of 1874 and 1876 the canton of Zurich cut the loops of the Limmat below Zurich and put the river between dams.
why: Below Zurich the Limmat made loops through wet meadows and bank forests. Each village built its own bank defences, often to push the water to the other bank. Floods damaged fields and roads, for example in 1846, 1874 and 1876. In June 1876 about a third of a normal year's rain fell in Zurich in six days.

Only three months after this flood, on 23 October 1876, the people of the canton of Zurich accepted a new water law. The canton now had to correct the large rivers (Rhine, Töss, Thur, Glatt, Limmat, Sihl), and paid with loans, money from the communes and a federal subsidy. The canton engineer Kaspar Wetli is named as the leading figure of this work.

On the Limmat the work started in 1880 with a cut at Schönenwerd. More cuts followed near Engstringen, Oetwil and Dietikon, and in 1896 the old bed at Dietikon was filled. After a flood in 1910 the dams were raised in 1912. Because land was expensive, the canton left almost no flood land between river and dams. Today houses, roads and railways stand on much of the old floodplain.
gained: The dams still protect the valley well today. A study for the Wettingen power plant found the flood safety largely guaranteed, and no dams must be raised.
The canton expected the lower groundwater level to raise the value of the land, mainly in the communes on the left bank. The work also gave jobs to unemployed people.
lost: Salmon used to swim up the Limmat until the late 19th century. The correction, power plants and pollution took away their basis of life.

The canalised river looks monotonous and has little natural variety of life. In 2002 a widening near Geroldswil was planned to give back a dynamic floodplain. A canton report of 2010 describes the revitalised floodplains at Dietikon and Geroldswil.

title: Glatt
place: Lake Greifen to the High Rhine
summary: The slow, marshy Glatt was straightened and deepened in several corrections, the third one in 1936 also to prepare for the airport at Kloten and new farmland.
why: The Glatt flows out of Lake Greifensee and has very little slope in its upper course. It wound through a wide area of moor and floodplain. Mills on the river were always in danger from high water. The city of Zurich controlled the river from the 15th century, and a first attempt to correct it came in 1593.

In 1807 the canton rejected a plan with dams on the sides (the 'Vogel project'). In 1812 the cantonal water police commission (an office that watched over rivers and water works) made an expert report, with help from Hans Conrad Escher. Workers dug a tunnel near Rheinsfelden and made the river straighter and deeper between Glattbrugg and Oberglatt. But in 1825 the money ran out and the work stopped. The project was closed in 1840.

The second correction came from 1878 to 1895. The third correction started in 1936. It prepared the ground for the planned airport at Kloten, for new houses and for melioration (work that makes wet land dry and good for farming). It also gave work to people without jobs. A last correction from Niederglatt to the Rhine in 1975 ended the old water power plants on the lower river.

Today the federal and cantonal authorities say that the corrections forced the Glatt into a narrow, deep and straight bed with hard banks. The river had flowed in bends through a wide area of moor and floodplain. That landscape was lost, and the river has large ecological problems. Since 2011, federal law tells the cantons to bring such rivers back to a more natural state. Projects at the airport and at other places now give the Glatt more space.
gained: The corrections served mainly flood protection and won farmland. Large drainage works came with them.
The third correction from 1936 prepared the ground for the planned airport at Kloten, for new houses and for melioration (work that makes wet land good for farming). It also created jobs.
lost: The Glatt once wound through a wide moor and floodplain landscape. With the correction this near-natural state was given up.
The river was forced into a narrow, deep and straight bed with hard banks. This left large ecological deficits in the river and the land beside it.
The old water works on the lower Glatt ended for good after the correction from Niederglatt to the Rhine in 1975.

text: The Glatt flows from Lake Greifen to the Rhine. In its upper part it has little slope, and mills on the river were always in danger from high water.

After an expert report of 1812 (with Hans Conrad Escher), workers dug a straight "Glatt canal" past Rümlang and deepened the river between Glattbrugg and Oberglatt. In 1825 the money ran out and the work stopped. The blue line is the straight canal, still the course of the Glatt today. The red line is the old winding bed east of it. Switch on the historical map of 1870 to see both.

title: Melchaa
summary: The Melchaa was led directly into Lake Sarnen, so the lake could catch its gravel.
why: The Grosse Melchaa first flowed north-east after it left its gorge. It joined the Sarneraa below the village of Sarnen. Its gravel blocked the Sarneraa, and it flooded Sarnen many times and badly.
Because of these repeated floods, the Grosse Melchaa was moved into Lake Sarnen in 1880. In 1880 the shore of the lake was at about the place of the railway bridge today.

The change had side effects. The gravel now builds a delta in the lake. The delta became longer and the slope of the river smaller, so the river can carry less gravel and its bed rises. In 2005 the bed in the lower part rose by about 1 m. Also, the area that drains into Lake Sarnen grew by almost one third. But the Sarneraa, the only outflow of the lake, has a small capacity. Lake Sarnen therefore floods more easily. In 2005 it reached a record level, and the Sarneraa flooded large parts of Sarnen.
gained: Before, the gravel of the Melchaa blocked the Sarneraa and caused more and more floods in Sarnen and on the lake shores. Leading it into the lake was a very successful measure.
The gravel built a large delta in the lake. Today the delta holds a very rare silver willow floodplain forest (Silberweiden-Auenwald).
lost: The growing delta made the river slope smaller, so the river carries less gravel. In 2005 its lower bed rose by about 1 m, and the river broke out.
The catchment area (land that drains into a lake) of Lake Sarnen grew by almost one third. The small outflow cannot keep up, so the lake floods more easily, for example in 2005.

title: Töss
summary: After the great floods of 1876 and 1877, Zurich planted forests and put the Töss into a narrow, secure bed.
why: In 1844 Gerold Meyer von Knonau called the Töss the most harmful river in the canton of Zurich. After heavy rain it rose fast, left its banks, covered the land with stones and tore away good soil. In dry times it often had almost no water.

In 1876 a very large flood caused huge damage along the Töss. Another flood came in 1877. The Zurich government then acted in two ways. It planted new forests in the area where the river starts, so that the soil holds more water. And from 1881 to 1910 it corrected the river between Steg and Dättlikon.

Step by step, the Töss got a straight and narrow bed. The aim was to control the river and to win new farmland. In a straight bed the river cuts down into the ground. To stop this, workers fixed the bed with almost 700 sills (low steps of stone or concrete across the river).

The canton says the correction protected the valley well: a flood as big as that of 1876 did little damage in 1953. But today the safety is no longer enough, and there is little space for more water. The sills are dangerous for people and stop fish from moving up the river. The straight bed is a poor home for plants and animals. In 2018 the canton and the communes made a plan to give the Töss a more natural form over the next decades.
gained: From the point of view of flood protection, the Töss correction proved its worth.
The correction tamed the river and won new farmland at the same time.
lost: To stop the bed from cutting down, almost 700 sills (low steps across the river) fixed it. They make fish migration up and down the river impossible, and their eddies are dangerous for people.
The monotonous bed is not a good home for water animals and plants.
Today the safety level no longer meets modern needs. In 2018 the canton made a plan to give the Töss a more natural form.

title: Werdenberg inland canal
place: Trübbach (Wartau) to Rüthi, beside the Alpine Rhine
summary: St. Gallen dug a canal on the land side of the new Rhine dams to collect the side streams, so that the dams had no gaps and the marshes of the Werdenberg plain could be drained.
why: Before the Rhine was corrected, many streams from the mountains flowed over the plain into the Alpine Rhine. Gravel raised the Rhine bed and the groundwater, so the farmland near the Rhine stayed wet. Floods were frequent from 1817 to 1890.

From 1862 St. Gallen built high dams along the Rhine, with one third of the cost paid by the Confederation. The dams needed to be closed. The engineer Jost Wey therefore built the inland canal in 1882–1886 to collect the side streams and bring them to the Rhine further down. The canal network then made land drainage possible, starting at Haag in 1885–1887.
The gain was new farmland. The loss was the wet meadows and marshes of the valley: HLS counts 6039 ha of valley marsh in 1890 and only 106 ha in 1999.
gained: The canal took in the side streams. So the Rhine dams had no more dangerous gaps at the stream mouths.
After the regulation, the Rhine broke out only once in a big way, in 1927, and on the Liechtenstein side. The St. Gallen plain stayed dry.
The canal network made land drainage possible. The works at Haag in 1885-1887 were the first large land drainage (melioration) in Switzerland.
lost: The wet meadows and valley marshes almost disappeared. In the Rhine valley, 6039 ha of valley marsh in 1890 shrank to 106 ha in 1999.
Later the Rhine bed sank, partly because of gravel mining. The groundwater sank too, and valuable groundwater streams (Giessen) dried up.
Since 2025, a revitalised stretch at Sevelen gives back some room. It has new channels and ponds for threatened fish such as grayling and nase.

title: Aare at Klingnau
place: Döttingen to the mouth of the Aare in the Rhine
summary: Aargau first put the wild lower Aare between dams, and in 1931–1935 a power station dammed it into the Klingnau reservoir.
why: Near its mouth the Aare once moved freely across a wide valley floor. It made many arms, gravel islands, reed beds and floodplain forests. In the 19th century many forests in the catchment were cut, so after heavy rain the water rose fast. Floods did a lot of damage.

From 1886 the canton of Aargau put the river step by step into a channel between dams (the HLS gives 1885–1904 for this correction). Behind the dams the old floodplains became dry. Then the Klingnau power station was built (1931–1935). It raised the Aare by 6.1 m and made a lake (a reservoir). On the map the lake is about 3 km long.

The slow water in the reservoir dropped huge amounts of fine mud. Shallow water and mud banks grew, and reeds and willows grew on them. Today the reservoir is a bird reserve of international importance, but the natural movement of the river is mostly gone.
gained: The Klingnau power station makes electricity. In 2023/24 it made about 212 million kWh, which is the use of about 46,000 households of four.
Mud settled in the slow water of the reservoir. Shallow water, mud banks and reeds grew, and the reservoir became a bird reserve of international importance.
Ornithologists (bird experts) have seen 346 bird species there, 93 of them on the Red List. On some winter days more than 2000 water birds stay there.
lost: The lower Aare valley had one of the largest floodplains of Switzerland. Behind the new dams from 1886, the old floodplains became dry.
The natural movement of the river is mostly gone. The old river arms fill up with mud, so people must dredge them to keep them open.
The old Aare arm at Machme was filled in when the power station was built. In 1995/1996 it was dug out again over 500 m.

title: Ticino
summary: A consortium put the Ticino into a straight canal through the Magadino plain (first phase 1888–1912). The plain was then drained and became farmland.
why: The Ticino and the streams that join it often flooded. The river also changed its bed again and again. In the Magadino plain this made marshes. For centuries the plain was almost empty, because people could not farm it and it was not healthy to live there. Malaria (a fever that mosquitoes carry) was known there from the 15th century and stayed a problem until the end of the 19th century.

Plans to correct the river go back to the early 19th century. Two events started the real work. In 1868 a very bad flood killed 41 people and caused more than 6 million francs of damage. In 1874 the railway from Locarno to Bellinzona opened across the plain.

The cantonal government made two projects. Parliament accepted them by a small majority, but the people voted no. The north of the canton (Sopraceneri) was for them, the south (Sottoceneri) was against. The government still set up a consortium in 1886: an association of the communes along the river. The correction was approved in 1885 and started in 1888. A first phase ended in 1912. The works went on, with breaks, into the 20th century (the HLS says until 1939) and cost more than 11 million francs.

The river now ran between dams. This made it possible to drain the plain in four big steps from 1918 to 1961. The Magadino plain became the largest farming area of the canton. Later, houses, roads, shops and the airfield also took much of the new land. In 1974 the canton protected the Bolle di Magadino at the river mouth as a nature reserve.
gained: The river now stayed in one bed between dams. This made it possible to drain the Magadino plain in four big steps from 1918 to 1961.
The Magadino plain became the largest farming zone of the canton of Ticino.
From the second half of the 20th century, firms, shops and the cantonal airfield also used the new land.
lost: A marsh landscape once covered the whole plain. Today only the last pieces are left, mainly at the Bolle di Magadino near the river mouth.
The wetlands of the plain changed into farmland and later into built-up land. In 1974 the canton protected the Bolle di Magadino as a nature reserve.

text: Before the work, the Ticino ran through the Magadino plain in a wide bed of gravel with many channels (red area). Its main channel (red line) moved with the floods. Much of the plain was marsh, and malaria (a fever that mosquitoes carry) was known there from the 15th century.
In 1868 a very bad flood killed 41 people. The railway across the plain opened in 1874. Both gave new force to plans for a correction.

title: Aire (Geneva)
place: Thairy (French border) to the Arve at Carouge
summary: The Aire was put into a straight canal in 1890–1940 to stop floods and to drain farmland; since 2002 Geneva has given parts of it a wide, natural bed again.
why: The Aire comes from France (Thairy) and flows through the plain of the Aire, past Lully and Confignon, to the Arve. Before the works it split into many channels in its upper part and made tight bends (meanders) at the foot of the Bernex–Confignon hill. From about 1860 people cut much forest on the Salève and the Mont-de-Sion. More gravel and mud came down, and the floods became worse than ever before.

Geneva wanted to protect the land from floods and to grow more food on it. The canton straightened the river from Thairy to the Lully bridge in 1890–1893. Between 1921 and 1940 it joined many small fields into larger ones (land consolidation), drained the plain and put the river into a canal down to the Arve. Later, in 1964–1970, the last part near La Praille was covered so that an industrial zone could grow.

The canal had side effects. In its upper part the bed was fixed by steps and strong dykes in the 1890s and lay higher than the land around it. There it was often dry in summer, and its ecology became very poor. In 2001 Geneva passed a law to renature (make natural again) the Aire. The works of 2002–2016 kept the old canal as a historical path and dug a wide new bed next to it, where the river can move freely. The project won the Landscape Award of the Council of Europe in 2019.
gained: The straight canal and the drainage of 1890-1940 served flood protection and farming. The plain of the Aire became cropland.
Near La Praille the canal was covered in 1964-1967. This let the industrial zone of La Praille grow over it.
Since the renaturation, the new wide bed protects people and goods against floods. In the ten-year flood of 2008, no flooding was reported.
lost: In its upper part the canal was fixed by steps and strong dykes and lay higher than the land. It was often dry for long periods in summer, and its ecology became very poor.
The banks were cut off from the river. Floodplain forests changed into forests of black locust (an invasive plant), and many floodplain species disappeared.
Since 2002 a wide new bed gives back some room. Rare birds such as the little ringed plover have come back, and so has the natterjack toad.

title: Maggia
place: Lower Maggia and its delta at Locarno
summary: A consortium built dams along the wild Maggia and led its mouth straight across the delta between Locarno and Ascona.
why: The Maggia is a wild mountain river. Its water level can rise very fast and very high. Over the centuries it often flooded. Log floating (sending tree trunks down the river) made the floods worse. The worst floods were at Cevio in 1648, with 52 dead, and in 1868, with 41 dead. At its mouth the river carries much gravel and sand into Lake Maggiore. There it builds a large delta that grows all the time, between Locarno and Ascona.

After the floods of 1868 the federal state got new powers. The 1874 constitution gave it the right to supervise water works in the mountains, and the 1877 federal law on water works followed. The federal environment office names the works on the Maggia from 1891 as one of the large corrections of that time.

From 1891 to 1930 a consortium (a group that shares the work and the cost) built dams along many parts of the river. The Maggia was never put into a full canal. A stone bridge between Losone and Solduno, built in 1815 and 1816, was half destroyed by a flood and repaired in 1887.

The dams did not stop all floods. In 1951 a flood destroyed the iron bridge at Ponte Brolla, and in 1978 a flood caused much damage. In 1949 the company Ofima got the right to use the river for hydropower. The delta mouth became a nature reserve in 1985.
gained: Strong dams protect villages and farmland from the force of the river. Many of these dams still work today.
From 1891 to 1930 a consortium built dams that hold the banks in many places. The river still has a branched bed with room to slow down floods.
lost: The dams, stone quarries and roads slowly took space from the river. They changed its natural movement in parts of the valley.

text: From 1891 to 1930 a consortium (a group of land owners and public bodies) built dams along the river. The Maggia was not put into a full canal, but its banks were secured in many places.
Across the delta the river was led in one straight course to the lake (blue line). It runs between the two old arms (red lines).

stops.title: The delta today
text: Today houses and farmland cover much of the delta, and since 1997 a farm at the mouth grows rice. The delta keeps growing into the lake: compare today's shore with the delta of 1870 (red area). The river mouth has been a nature reserve since 1985.
The dams did not stop all floods: in 1951 and 1978 the river did great damage again.

title: Rheintal inland canal
place: Sennwald to St. Margrethen (into the Old Rhine)
summary: As part of the international Rhine regulation, Switzerland dug a canal through the lower St. Gallen Rhine valley that collects the side streams and drains the plain into the Old Rhine.
why: The lower Rhine valley was flat and wet. Floods of the Rhine in 1868 in the St. Gallen Rhine valley and 1890 in Vorarlberg led Switzerland and Austria to sign the treaty of 1892 on the international Rhine regulation.

The treaty led to the Fussach cut (1900) and the Diepoldsau cut (1923). Each country had to build the inland canals on its own bank. On the Swiss side this was the Rheintal inland canal, built under the engineer Jost Wey. Because the Rhine now ran to Fussach, the canal could use the old Rhine bed below St. Margrethen as its outlet.

The canal made land drainage possible and turned the marshes into farmland. It needed drop structures at Lienz, Blatten and Montlingen, which also make electricity. Today the area is built up, and floods in 1999 and 2013 showed that the canal is now too small in places.
gained: The canal collects many side streams that once flowed across the plain. It was meant to drain the whole plain from St. Margrethen to Sennwald.
The state treaty of 1892, of which the canal was part, aimed to remove flood danger and marshland on both banks of the Rhine.
lost: The marshes of the valley floor almost disappeared. In the Rhine valley, 6039 ha of valley marsh in 1890 shrank to 106 ha in 1999.
Today the canal is too small in places. Near Rüthi and Widnau it cannot carry big floods, and floods in 1999 and 2013 damaged homes and industry.

stops.title: One canal for all streams
text: In 1892 Switzerland and Austria signed a treaty to regulate the Rhine. The Rhine got a new mouth at Fussach in 1900. Its old bed from St. Margrethen to the lake became free.

From 1896 to 1906 Switzerland dug the Rheintal inland canal (blue). It starts at Sennwald, collects the side streams and flows into the Old Rhine at St. Margrethen. The peat and floods during the work made it hard and expensive.

title: Alpine Rhine (Rüthi–Lake Constance)
summary: Switzerland and Austria cut two big bends of the Rhine, at Fussach (1900) and Diepoldsau (1923), and moved its mouth into Lake Constance, to make the river shorter, faster and safer.
why: Below Au the Rhine made long bends before it reached Lake Constance at Altenrhein. On this long, flat way the water lost speed and dropped its gravel. The bed rose, and the land beside the river became wet. Big floods hit the St. Gallen Rhine valley in 1868, and the Austrian (Vorarlberg) side in 1888 and 1890.

The river is the border between Switzerland and Austria. One cut would lie in Austria, the other in Switzerland, so each state had to give something. Plans for cuts existed since 1792. Talks between the two states started in 1824, after the floods of 1817 and 1821. But for almost 70 years the two states did not agree.

After the floods of 1888 and 1890 they signed a state treaty in 1892. It created the International Rhine Regulation (IRR), and the two states share the cost of its works. The IRR built the Fussach cut (1895-1900) and the Diepoldsau cut (1910-1923). The two cuts made the river about 10 km shorter, and the mouth moved east from Altenrhein to Fussach. Treaties of 1924 and 1954 added the dams into the lake and a narrower middle channel.
The cuts made the valley much safer, but the river lost its natural banks. Today the IRR and the two states plan the project Rhesi to give the river more room again.
gained: The cuts made the river about 10 km shorter (Fussach 7 km, Diepoldsau 3 km). The faster water carried its gravel away better, so the bed rose less.
With the Diepoldsau cut, the danger of big floods on the valley floor ended for a long time. Prosperity then came to the St. Gallen Rhine valley.
lost: The cut was nearly an ecological disaster for the Rhine, says a local historian. Fish numbers fell sharply, and most of the floodplain forest disappeared.
The cut separated the Diepoldsau loop from the river. It became the Old Rhine (Alter Rhein), a still water used for leisure.

The safety is not complete. The dams hold only a 100-year flood. A big flood today could cause damage of up to 13 billion francs (another IRR page says 14 billion). Project Rhesi will widen the river.

stops.title: The old mouth at Altenrhein
text: Until 1900 the Rhine flowed from Au north to Brugg, then west past St. Margrethen and Gaissau, and through Rheineck into Lake Constance at Altenrhein. On this long way the water lost speed, and the gravel raised the bed.

Plans for a shorter course existed since 1792. In 1838 Friedrich Wilhelm Hartmann proposed a cut from Lustenau straight to Fussach. The red line is the old course just before the work. Switch on the historical map of 1895 to see it.

stops.title: The Fussach cut
text: The state treaty of 1892 between Switzerland and Austria-Hungary created the International Rhine Regulation (IRR). In 1895-1900 the IRR dug a new, straight bed of about 5 km in Austria, from Höchst and Lustenau to the lake at Fussach. It made the river about 7 km shorter.
The old Rhine to Altenrhein became a quiet side water. Today it takes the water of the Rhine valley inland canal (built 1895-1906).

stops.title: The loop at Diepoldsau
text: Upstream, the Rhine still made a big loop to the east around Diepoldsau, close to Hohenems. Here too the river bed kept rising.
The 1892 treaty also planned a second cut here. The red line follows the loop as it was before the work began. Switch on the historical map of 1905 to see its gravel banks.

lines.name: Rhine loop around Diepoldsau (until 1923, traced on the 1905 map)

stops.title: The Diepoldsau cut
text: In 1910-1923 the IRR dug a straight new bed west of Diepoldsau, from Kriessern to Widnau. The First World War delayed the work. On 18 April 1923 the water first flowed through the cut. It made the river about 3 km shorter.

The old loop became the 'Alter Rhein', a quiet water. Since then Diepoldsau lies between the new Rhine and the old loop, which is still the border with Austria. A new treaty in 1924 settled the further works.

lines.name: Rhine loop around Diepoldsau (until 1923)
Diepoldsau cut (1910-1923)

stops.title: Today and the Rhesi project
text: The mouth was pushed into the lake with new dams (1924-1934 and since 1972), so that the gravel goes to deep water. A treaty of 1954 made the middle channel narrower, so that the water flows faster and carries the gravel away.

The dams are still too weak for the biggest floods. In the project Rhesi, Switzerland and Austria will widen the river bed on 26 km, from the Ill mouth to the lake, for more safety and more nature. The new state treaty came into force on 1 July 2025. In May 2026 the project was submitted for approval in Austria and for preliminary review in Switzerland. It will cost about CHF 2 billion.

title: Sense (lower course)
summary: Around 1900 the lower Sense between Thörishaus and Laupen was straightened and held in a narrow bed by wooden walls. This protected villages and roads and won farmland.
why: The lower Sense runs between the cantons of Bern and Fribourg. On the map of 1880 it has a wide bed of gravel with several channels. Big floods are known from 1852, 1902, 1927 and 2007.

People built single wooden walls along the banks from 1725 on, near villages, roads and fields. Around 1900 the river was straightened and channelled in one large correction. Between Heitibüffel and Laupen both banks got wooden walls, rolls of wire and stones, and iron posts; flood dykes further back followed in the first half of the 20th century.

The straight river flowed faster and dug its bed deeper (bed erosion). From about 1950 people built stone steps (sills) across the river to stop this; today there are 46 of them. The new land is good farmland, but the river lost its natural banks. The cantons of Bern and Fribourg are now working on a development plan for the river (project Sense21).
gained: The straightening and channelling around 1900 won extra land. This land is mostly safe from floods and is now highly productive farmland.
lost: The straight river carried more gravel and dug its bed deeper (bed erosion). Since about 1950, people built stone sills to fix the bed; today there are 46.
From Thörishaus down, the Sense is strongly channelled and has few gravel banks. The natural floodplain dynamics are almost gone in the lower course.
The former floodplain forests have mostly changed into beech forests during the last century.

Gained/lost: The source also reports falling brown trout numbers and that the nase has not been seen in the Sense since 1993, but it says no clear cause for the fish decline was found; so fish are not listed as a loss of the correction. title: Vedeggio at Agno
place: Bioggio to the delta at Agno (Lake Lugano)
summary: From 1906 the Vedeggio was taken out of its winding bed through Agno and put into a straight canal across the Piano d'Agno, which made the plain usable for farms and later for the airport of Lugano.
why: Flat land is rare in Ticino. On the map of 1905 the Vedeggio moves over gravel banks on the Piano d'Agno, at its mouth into Lake Lugano. Drainage of the plain had started in the 19th century.
In 1906 the correction of the Vedeggio began. The river was put into a straight canal, and the drained plain gave the commune of Agno much more productive land, first for farming.
After 1945 the plain filled with industry, shops and the airport of Lugano. Today the Confederation, the canton and the communes pay for new flood protection on the Vedeggio.
gained: The correction from 1906 and the drainage of the Piano d'Agno greatly increased the productive land of Agno. At first it became a large farming area.
After the Second World War, industry and trade grew fast on the plain. Since 1980 the airport of Agno has had scheduled flights.
lost: The Vedeggio mouth is no longer a natural delta. Today the nearby Magliasina mouth is the only natural delta left on Lake Lugano.
The old canal is now too small in critical places. Since 2006 a consortium has been building new flood protection; works worth about 34 million francs were done by July 2024.

Story stop 3: 'raising the dikes again against a 100-year flood' not found in the 2024 report; replaced by the report's statement that the protection works at Agno, Muzzano and Bioggio are done.
