title: Thur in the Toggenburg
summary: St. Gallen straightened and dammed the upper Thur between Ebnat-Kappel and Lichtensteig in 1907–1913. Today Wattwil reaches over the old river loops.
why: On the map of 1900 the upper Thur made loops and gravel banks in the flat valley floor around Wattwil. How often the fields there were flooded is not confirmed by a source.

Further down, Thurgau and Zurich had corrected the Thur in 1874–1893. In 1907–1913 the canton of St. Gallen followed with its own correction between Ebnat-Kappel and Lichtensteig. The exact aims of this work are not confirmed by a source we could open.
Today streets and buildings of Wattwil lie where the loops were. The corrected bed keeps digging deeper, and the canal is now worn out.
lost: The bed of the corrected river keeps digging deeper (bed erosion). This makes the bank erosion worse and lowers the groundwater.
The bed has eroded by up to 1 m. The river lacks dynamic habitats such as gravel banks, backwaters and pools.
After more than 100 years the canal is worn out. A 100-year flood could now flood large parts of the centre of Wattwil.

title: Seymaz
place: Marshes of Rouelbeau and Sionnet down to the Bochet bridge
summary: From 1909 to 1924 Geneva drained the marshes of the Seymaz plain and put the stream into a straight canal of about 5 km, to win farmland.
why: The Seymaz is a small river east of Geneva. Before 1915 large marshes covered its upper plain. The marshes of Sionnet and Rouelbeau were separated only by wet meadows. Farmers came to cut litter for their animals there.

In the early 20th century Geneva wanted more land for crops. The canton made plans to join small fields into larger ones and to drain the marshes. The first drains were dug in 1909–1914; the large works came in 1915–1924 (the river sheet says 1915–1925). The marshes were dried, the Seymaz was put into a straight canal with a very low slope, and small side streams were put into pipes under the ground.

The new fields were good, but many plants and animals of the marsh disappeared. Before, the marshes stored water and evened out the flow. Later, floods became a problem in the town and in the country. The 1998 bill names growing towns, drainage and modern farming with heavy machines as causes. Since a law of 1998, Geneva has been giving the Seymaz a natural bed again near Rouelbeau and has made a new wetland in the old Sionnet marsh.
gained: The drainage and the canal enlarged the cropland of the canton. New square fields replaced the marsh.
lost: The big marshes of Choulex, Meinier, Sionnet and others disappeared. Before, they stored water and evened out the flow of the river.
Hedges and trees were removed. The rigid canal had little room for plants and animals, and its concrete bed left almost no life for fish.
The drained peat soil sank by about one metre. This made hollows that flood easily.
Since about 2000 the renaturation gives back some room. The Sionnet marshes (2005-2006) can store about 800,000 m3 of water, and rare marsh plants have come back.

The marsh outlines are traced by eye on the 1913 map and are approximate. Only the upper Seymaz around Choulex is drawn; the downstream stretch to Chêne-Bourg is not traced. The exact years of each renaturation stage were not checked. Gained/lost: Conflict with the current 'why' text: the 1998 bill (§ 3.4) explains the later floods by urbanisation and modern farming with heavy machines, not by the loss of the marsh. The Geneva river sheet (Fiche-rivière no 10) says the marshes once evened out the flow, and that the restored Sionnet marshes removed the flood danger in the urban part by end of 2009. The ground sinking is attributed in the bill to the compaction of drained peat (paraphrased by the fetch tool; the exact 'peat' wording was not seen). The fish quote refers to the canalised, concrete-bed stretch. Sources check: Canal length: the river sheet says 'more than 5 km', the 1998 bill gives 4750 m still canalised upstream of the Bochet bridge; summary changed from 'almost 5 km' to 'about 5 km'. Main works: bill 1915–1924, river sheet 1915–1925 (both named). 'Cattle grazing' removed (only litter cutting found). Flood causes: the bill also names systematic drainage, added.

title: Drainage of the Rhône plain (Fully–Saillon)
place: Rhône plain between Riddes, Saillon, Fully and Martigny
summary: After the Rhône was embanked, the low plain between Riddes and Martigny stayed wet; in 1910–1940 drainage canals and land consolidation turned it into farmland and orchards.
why: The first Rhône correction (from 1863) held the river between dykes, but it did not dry the plain. Behind the dykes the water stayed in the low land. Springs such as the Sarvaz near Saillon made a large pond, the 'Grande Gouille', for months each year. The land was unhealthy and could not be farmed.

In 1873 the canton made a plan for a system of main and side canals that lead the water back into the Rhône far downstream. Most of the work came after the First World War. Between Riddes and Martigny the communes formed a consortium (a group that shares the work and the costs). Experts sorted every plot into four classes of wetness, and owners of wetter land paid more. In the plain of Saillon the fields were joined, drained and irrigated in 1914–1922.
The new land was farmed and planted with trees, and many houses were built on it. The old marshes, with their rich plants and animals, almost disappeared.
gained: The drainage canals dried the low land behind the Rhône dykes. The Grande Gouille, a pond that covered the plain for months each year, was drained in 1919-1920.
By the mid-20th century the plain was well farmed and full of orchards. Many houses were built on it.
lost: The marshes of the Sarvaz, called the 'Valais Camargue', almost disappeared. Naturalists of the time regretted the loss of their rich plants and animals.
Old uses of the wetland ended. The reed harvests and the wild 'islands' of thorny bushes, a paradise for pheasants, were almost all gone.
People built houses in the plain that the Rhône can flood. This raised the damage a dyke break could cause.

title: Suze (Schüss) in the Vallon de Saint-Imier
place: Vallon de Saint-Imier (shown: Courtelary to Cortébert)
summary: Between 1910 and 1940 a good third of the Suze (Schüss) was put into a canal. In the Vallon de Saint-Imier the maps show that its bends between Courtelary and Cortébert were cut.
why: The Suze (German: Schüss) flows from the Jura down the Vallon de Saint-Imier to Lake Biel. In the 17th and 18th centuries it drove about 40 mills, forges and other works; later watch firms and other industry grew along it. On the map of 1905 it made bends through wet meadows in the flat parts of the valley.

In Biel a straight arm of the river, the Schüss canal, was built from 1825 through the new quarters. Between 1910 and 1940 a good third of the river's length was canalised. The reasons are not confirmed by a source; the railway (1874), villages and farmland along the river may have played a role.
A plan of the canton of Bern of 1998 asks for more natural banks and better flood protection along the Suze.

That the Courtelary–Cortébert stretch belongs to the 1910-1940 works is my reading of the maps (bends in 1905, straight bed in 1946), not a written source. Only this stretch is drawn. The reasons (villages, railway, farmland) are general, not stated in the HLS article. Gained/lost: Thin. The habitat statement is from a 2022 ZHAW thesis about the Schüss canal in Biel (built from 1825), not about the Vallon. No gained item, because no source states flood protection or farmland gains for this river. Removed by review: the habitat item was about the Suze canal in Biel, not the Vallon. Sources check: Reasons for the 1910–1940 works (villages, railway, farming) and drainage of the valley floor are not in the HLS; marked as not confirmed or turned into map observations. '40 mills for centuries' narrowed to the 17th and 18th centuries (HLS).

title: Muota
summary: After the flood of 1910 the Muota was corrected in two stretches (HLS: 1911–1926), in the Muota valley and on the plain from Ibach to Brunnen.
why: The Muota flows from the Muotatal through the Schwyz valley basin and into Lake Lucerne at Brunnen. It damaged its valley many times. Its flood plain kept the village of Brunnen on the hill sides for a long time. From the 15th century, groups of land owners built and kept river banks, and the river was slowly forced into a fixed bed.
The last big flood came in June 1910. In the commune of Muotathal it destroyed 7 bridges, 11 houses and 4 stables, and many people became very poor.

In 1910 the canton of Schwyz accepted a federal subsidy for the work. With this, the canton took on the duty to build the works and to keep them in good condition. In the years after 1910 the canton built up the Muota from above Muotatal down to the lake. The federal state, the canton and the district of Schwyz paid subsidies. The land owners who had a benefit paid the rest. In 1922 the district also asked the Korporation Uri to pay, because it owned alps in the Muota area in the canton of Uri. Uri said no, and the Federal Council decided in favour of Uri. In 1931 the Federal Court did not hear the appeal of Schwyz.

A Wuhrkorporation (a group of land owners who must keep the river dams in good condition) was founded and kept the dams. Today the district of Schwyz plans to give the Muota a more natural bed near the old Brunnen power plant.
gained: After the works, a group of land owners kept the dams in good condition. From then on, the dams prevented floods like the one of 1910.
The works also protected the road through the Muota valley.
lost: The river lost much of its natural form. Today the district of Schwyz plans to restore natural functions and a more natural bed near the old Brunnen power plant.

title: Aare canal at Gösgen
summary: A weir at Winznau sends most of the Aare into a straight canal of about 5 km to the Gösgen power station; the old loop of the river gets only a little water.
why: Below Olten the Aare made a wide loop to the south, past Schachen and Obergösgen. A canal across this loop could use the fall of the river to make electricity.
From 1913 to 1917 a canal was dug from a weir at Winznau to a power station at Niedergösgen. The station started in November 1917. The canal cuts off the loop. It is about 4.8 km long.

Since then most of the water flows through the canal. The old loop ("Alte Aare") gets only the water that does not go into the canal. The power station was renewed in 1997–2000. With the new concession, the old Aare is to get more water, for nature.
gained: The Gösgen power station makes about 300 million kWh of electricity per year. This is enough for about 66,500 households.
lost: Most of the Aare now flows through the canal. The old loop (Alte Aare) gets only the water that does not go into the canal.

Many works have strongly reduced the natural variety of the bank habitats here. Under the new concession, the old Aare is to get more water. The proposal is 12 m³/s in winter and at least 20 m³/s in summer.

title: Saane (Sarine)
place: Montbovon to Lac de la Gruyère
summary: The wide gravel bed of the Saane in the Intyamon valley was narrowed to gain farmland (HLS: 1917–1987). Further down, the Rossens dam (1948) made the Lac de la Gruyère.
why: In the Intyamon valley the Saane flows over a flat valley floor. On the map of 1900 it spreads over a wide bed of gravel with many arms. How much land the floods took from farmers is not confirmed by a source.

At the end of the 19th century large works near Enney corrected the bed of the Saane and gave more land to farmers. The federal law of 1877 made federal money for river works more common. The HLS table dates the correction from Montbovon to the Lac de la Gruyère to 1917–1987. Details of these works and who carried them out are not confirmed.

River corrections in Switzerland usually put the river between dams and closed its side arms, and they drained many floodplains. In the Intyamon a floodplain of national importance remains: Les Auges d'Estavannens (54 ha). How much gravel habitat was lost here is not confirmed.
gained: At the end of the 19th century, works on the bed of the Saane near Enney gave more land to farmers.
The Rossens dam (1948) makes the Lac de la Gruyère. The lake feeds the Hauterive power station. It makes on average 280 million kWh of electricity per year.
lost: The Lac de la Gruyère covered the hamlet of Pont-en-Ogoz. Today only the ruins of its castle stand out of the water.
The lake also flooded the old Thusy power station in 1948.
In Switzerland, river corrections drained many floodplains (Auen). In the Intyamon, Les Auges d'Estavannens is still a floodplain of national importance.

title: Bünz
summary: After the First World War the canton of Aargau straightened the Bünz from Muri to Othmarsingen (1919–1942) and drained the marshes of the valley to grow more food.
why: The valley floor of the Bünz is almost flat. The stream wound through it and often flooded wide areas. Much of the land was marsh and could not be used for farming for most of the year. People had wanted a correction for almost 50 years.

The First World War showed that Switzerland had to grow more of its own food. In March 1918 the Aargau government wrote that protecting fertile land from floods and turning marsh into fields was now a first duty of the state. Between 1919 and 1942 the Bünz was straightened from Muri to Othmarsingen, and the wet land was drained.

The new bed had a trapezoid shape and banks of stone blocks or concrete. In Othmarsingen it could carry 60 m³/s instead of 20 m³/s. But the stream became a straight, dull channel with little life. The last part, from Möriken to Wildegg, was not corrected because of the cost. There a flood in May 1999 made a new wild floodplain, the Bünzaue, which is now protected.
gained: In Othmarsingen, the new bed could carry 60 m³/s of water instead of 20 m³/s. This protected the fertile land from floods.
The marshes were drained and became farmland. Before, the wet land could not be used for farming for most of the year.
lost: The Bünz lost its many meanders. It was forced into a straight bed with hard banks.
The hard banks stopped almost all bank erosion. The new bed had no structures that give fish a habitat or a place to hide.
The stream became a dull, straight channel. Since 2004, several projects have given parts of the Bünz a more natural bed again.

title: Wägitaler Aa (Wägitalersee)
summary: A dam on the Wägitaler Aa made a reservoir for electricity in 1924; the old village of Innerthal went under water.
why: In the upper Wägital the Aa flowed through a flat valley floor with the village of Innerthal, its church, farms and, from 1861, a small spa. People had discussed a power station here since the late 19th century. In 1909 the city of Zurich bought the spa hotel, also to secure the water.

Electricity use in Switzerland grew fast. A dam was finished in 1924, and the water began to fill the valley in July 1924. The church of the old village was blown up in August 1924. The water drives the Rempen power station lower down the valley, mostly in winter.

The planned resettlement was only partly done. Sixteen new houses were built on the slope, and a new church and school above the lake. More than 100 people left the commune. Innerthal had 363 people in 1900 and only 223 in 1930.
gained: The lake stores 150 million m³ of water. Most of it makes electricity in winter.
In recent times, the fish-rich lake and the landscape of the valley have helped tourism.
lost: The water covered the old village of Innerthal, with 37 homes and 498 ha of meadows, pastures, fields and forest. The church was blown up in August 1924.
The planned resettlement was only partly done. More than 100 people had to leave the commune.
The law requires the power plant to reduce strong changes in flow (hydropeaking) by 2030. It must also restore free fish migration.

title: Sihl (Sihlsee reservoir)
place: Sihl valley between Euthal and the dam north of Einsiedeln
summary: The Sihl was dammed north of Einsiedeln; the reservoir drowned a high valley of farms and moors to make electricity for the railways.
why: Near Einsiedeln the Sihl wound through a wide, flat high valley with moors, meadows and many farms. Since 1897 the canton of Schwyz, the district of Einsiedeln and the cantons of Zurich and Zug talked about a reservoir there. They argued about payments, cheap electricity, new roads and compensation for the farmers.

From 1932 to 1937 the Etzelwerk company, owned by the Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) and the NOK power company, built the dam. Its supporters spoke of new jobs and of Swiss self-supply with electricity. The water goes to a power station at Altendorf on Lake Zurich and makes electricity for the railways.

The lake covered 943 ha of productive farmland. According to the HLS, 452 farm businesses were affected. Only part of the families (about a third, says the National Museum) got a new home near the lake. The reservoir also changed the Sihl below it: it takes away water, but it also reduces flood peaks.
gained: The Etzelwerk makes on average 270 million kWh of electricity per year for the railways.
The reservoir reduces flood peaks on the Sihl. In winter it also keeps the river bed from drying out.
lost: The lake covered 943 ha of productive land. 452 farm businesses were affected.
Before the flooding, 93 houses, 124 barns with stables and 179 peat huts were cleared. Only about a third of the families got a new home near the lake.
The lake drowned a landscape of moors and meadows. About 45% of the area was peat and bog, and 41% was pasture and meadow.
The power station takes water away from the Sihl. Less water in the river makes the water quality worse.

title: Aare between Wildegg and Brugg
summary: For the Wildegg–Brugg power station the Aare was dammed at Schinznach Bad and most of its water was sent into an artificial canal to Brugg.
why: Between Wildegg and Brugg the Aare flowed in a natural bed with many arms. In floods the bed was up to 500 m wide, and the arms changed again and again. The valley floor near Villnachern was gravel, islands and floodplain forest.

From 1949 to 1953 the Wildegg–Brugg power station was built. It is the largest power station on the Aare. A weir at Schinznach Bad holds the river back, and a canal takes most of the water to the power house near Brugg. The HLS says the work brought "great changes to the landscape".

The old river bed (the "Alte Aare") now gets only a part of the water. In the 20 years before 2015 the canton of Aargau has made new side arms and gravel areas there, as part of its floodplain park (Auenschutzpark).
gained: The Wildegg–Brugg power station is the largest hydropower station on the Aare.
Its construction from 1949 to 1953 also brought some jobs to Villnachern.
lost: The Aare lost its natural bed with many changing arms, which was up to 500 m wide in floods. The power station strongly canalised the river.
The old Aare gets a minimum of only 10 m³/s of water all year. More water reaches it only in floods above 430 m³/s.
Floods that floodplain forests need are now possible only along the old Aare. In the 20 years before 2015, the canton restored this stretch in several steps.

title: Areuse
summary: The Areuse in the Val-de-Travers was corrected in 1867–1869 and again from 1949; the second correction straightened the river between Couvet and Travers.
why: The Val-de-Travers has a flat valley floor with good farmland. In 1867–1869 the Areuse was corrected a first time. In the upper half of the valley it was put into a canal, and rows of poplars were planted to help dry the land.

From 1949 the river was corrected again. The HLS table of river corrections gives 1949–1955 for the stretch Travers–Couvet; the HLS article on the Areuse gives 1949–1984 for the works. In the same period, small fields in the valley were joined into larger ones (1929–1989).
For farmers and older people the canal stands for safety against floods and for good farmland. Today the canton also restores parts of the Areuse to make them more natural, for example at Môtiers.

Removed unsourced reasons (marsh, frequent floods, 'after the Second World War the canton ... to protect the villages'). Added the 2015 landscape-quality report (canalisation in 1868 with poplars to dry the land; farmers see the canal as safety). The 1867–1869 canalisation in that report concerns the upper half of the valley, not Couvet–Travers. HLS dates differ (1949–1955 in the table, 1949–1984 in the Areuse article); both given.

title: Inn and Flaz at Samedan
place: Punt Muragl and Samedan to Bever (Inn up to Zuoz)
summary: The Inn in the Upper Engadine was put between dikes at the end of the 19th century, the Flaz and Inn at Samedan were squeezed into a closed canal after the floods of 1951 and 1954, and in 2004 the Flaz got a new 4 km bed away from the village.
why: Samedan lies where the Flaz meets the Inn. The Flaz joined the Inn above the village, so floods of both rivers put Samedan in great danger. The Inn flooded the Upper Engadine in 1566, 1951 and other years.

At the end of the 19th century the Inn was corrected between Samedan and Zuoz, and dikes were built around the village. After the floods of 1951 and 1954 the dikes were raised and both rivers were squeezed into a closed canal. But in July 1987 the village only just escaped a disastrous flood.

Instead of raising the dikes again, Samedan and the canton chose a new solution: in 2002-2005 the Flaz was moved away from the village into a new bed through the plain, with 75% of the money from the Confederation and the canton. It was the first relocation of a larger Swiss river in more than 80 years, and it also gave new habitat to plants and animals. Downstream, the Inn near Bever was given a natural bed again in two stages until 2020.
gained: The new bed of the Flaz (2002–2005) took the river away from the village. It made Samedan safe from floods.
The new Flaz created more than 3.5 km of new river habitat. Brown trout, grayling and minnow are expected to live there.
lost: After the floods of 1951 and 1954, the Flaz and the Inn were squeezed into a closed canal along the village. The Inn left its natural course in the valley floor.
Behind the high dikes the risk grew. In July 1987 the water came within about 20 cm of the top of the dikes.
Because of the flood danger, the canton later set building rules and, in part of the village, a building ban.
Near Bever, dikes on both sides had narrowed the Inn. Since a restoration in two stages until 2020, the river can spread out freely again.

title: Lorze (Baar plain)
summary: In 1973–1974 the Lorze got a new, shorter bed from Baar straight to Lake Zug near the town of Zug; part of the old bed became the motorway.
why: The Lorze is the main river of the canton of Zug. Below Baar it flowed west across the flat Baar plain and reached Lake Zug between Zug and Cham. In floods, for example in 1861, 1910 and 1934, it covered the low land.

In the 19th and 20th centuries people built canals and dams along the Lorze, for water power and against floods. The motorway N4a needed the old river bed at Baar. So in 1973 and 1974 the canton gave the river a new bed from Baar south-west to the lake, and part of the old bed was used for the motorway.

Even earlier, in 1591–1592, Jost Knopfli of Zug deepened the outlet of the lake (also the Lorze) at Cham. The HLS says this lowered Lake Zug by about 2.5 m. That work happened long before the first maps of this series.
gained: The new bed was built mainly to carry flood water away safely. At the same time, flood protection got better and the plain was drained on a large scale.
Part of the old river bed was used for the motorway. Because the motorway took this northern route, it did not go through the lake shore landscape.
lost: Over 3.8 km the new Lorze got a very straight bed. It was built for water flow more than for nature and landscape.
The old Lorze was cut off from its water and became a small trickle. Only two small side streams and drainage water from the motorway feed it.
The new bed has no bays, flat banks or gravel banks and looks canalised. In 2006 the canton government proposed to widen it near Baar and to lead water back into the old Lorze.

title: Reuss plain (Aargau)
summary: The Reusstal renovation corrected the river, drained the valley floor for farming and created the Flachsee nature reserve.
why: In the Aargau Reuss valley the river made many bends. The flat valley floor suffered from floods and from changes of the river bed. People built bank protection from the 16th century, but it helped little. Plans to make the Reuss straight, for example by Hans Conrad Gyger in 1648 and by Johann Gottfried Tulla in 1809, were never built. Corrections from about 1840 did not last. In the 19th century, flood dams were built from Mühlau to Rottenschwil.

In 1953 a dam broke at Merenschwand and the flood caused heavy damage. This started a new plan. The first plans would have dried the land for farming and destroyed the wetlands. Nature protection groups were against them, because the valley was an important wetland. In 1962 they founded the Stiftung Reusstal (a foundation to protect the Reuss valley).

In 1963 the foundation started a popular initiative, 'Freie Reuss'. In 1965 the people of Aargau accepted it with a large majority. It stopped new power plants on the Reuss below Bremgarten. In 1969 the people accepted the 'Reusstalgesetz' by a small majority. This law joined the river work with nature protection.

From 1971 to 1985 the Reusstalsanierung (the renewal of the Reuss valley) was carried out. It was a project of several cantons that changed the course of the river and drained and improved the land. Agriculture, the electricity industry and nature protection groups all took part. In 1975 the new Bremgarten-Zufikon power plant dammed the river, and the Flachsee was formed. It is now a well-known nature reserve for birds. The power plant also limited the natural movement of the river.
gained: The renewal aimed at safe flood protection and more efficient farming. Today dams protect the plain, and canals with pumping stations drain it.
Nature reserves were set up next to the farmland. The floodplain area of the Reuss plain covers 327 ha, the largest in the Aargau floodplain park.
The Flachsee formed in 1975 when the new power plant raised the water. It is a reserve of national importance for water birds and migrating birds.
lost: The power plant of 1975 further limited the natural movement of the river. At Bremegrien, the canton removed bank stones over 700 m in 2003, so the river can shape its bank again.
Before 1975, about two thirds of the area of today's Flachsee was forest. The rest was farmland.
In the upper Aargau Reuss plain, permanently wet habitats strongly declined, because the groundwater level went down.
After the Reuss valley law came into force, farming in the valley became much more intensive.

notes: Not in the HLS table. Length of the corrected stretch not found. Round 2: the river course in this stretch changed little between 1870 and today, so no older main channel is drawn; the red line is the cut-off loop "Stille Reuss" traced on the 1960 map (also visible in 1870). The Flachsee outline is read from the 1960/today maps and is approximate. The 1965 vote count differs between Stiftung Reusstal papers, so no number is given. Gained/lost: Gained 1 combines a stated aim (1987 Stiftung Reusstal booklet, quoting the project goals) with the present state (Flachsee info sheet); the dams themselves date partly from the 19th century. Lost 3 ('diese' = permanently wet biotopes) is from a slide-style 2022 presentation of the Stiftung Reusstal; it does not give a date for the groundwater drop. Lost 4: the 1987 booklet says the intensification happened 'ganz allgemein und reusstalprojektunabhängig' as well, so it is not caused by the project alone. The Kleine Reuss was put into a pipe in the 1970s and opened again in 2004 (canton flyer); not used, to keep items short. The 1987 booklet text is two-column OCR, so the lost 4 quote is joined across columns. Sources check: why 2: 'first plans were only technical' kept as 'would have destroyed the wetlands' (Stiftung Reusstal 2022, 'Biotop-Kahlschlag'). Stop 4: 'old loops are kept as ponds' removed (no source). HLS confirms Gyger 1648, Tulla 1809, c. 1840 corrections and 1971–1985 cross-cantonal project. The 1987 booklet is two-column OCR; some quotes joined across columns.
